```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center", dpi = 110)
```

**Question:** what makes commuters outside Sweden's metropolitan regions choose the car over public transport? How well can that choice be predicted?

**Data:** 2,475 commuters. Each record has:
- the chosen mode (car or public transport);
- door-to-door travel times by public transport and by car, and their ratio;
- trip and public-transport service characteristics (all dummies):
  - one or multiple transfers;
  - a walk of **more than** 500 m to the nearest stop;
  - a transfer wait of more than 5 minutes;
  - high frequency (more than 8 departures per hour);
  - a trip distance over 20 km;
- demographics: age, gender, high income, high education.

**Approach:**
- A random forest with `mtry` tuned on the out-of-bag error.
- Compared with a logistic regression, the classic discrete-choice benchmark.
- Evaluated with metrics that account for the class imbalance: most commuters drive.

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)
library(pROC)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
```

## 1. Data

```{r data}
load("data/TransportModeSweden.RData")   # data frame `data`
transport <- data |>
  mutate(across(c(time_pt, time_car, time_ratio), ~ as.numeric(gsub(",", ".", .x))),  # decimal commas
         mode = factor(mode, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("public", "car")))
cat("missing values per column:\n"); print(colSums(is.na(transport))[colSums(is.na(transport)) > 0])
transport <- transport[complete.cases(transport), ]
cat(nrow(transport), "complete cases\n")
round(prop.table(table(transport$mode)), 3)
```

The data is imbalanced: about 4 in 5 commuters drive. A model that always predicts "car" is already about 80% accurate, so accuracy alone says little. Balanced accuracy (the mean of the two class-wise hit rates) and AUC are reported alongside it.

```{r eda, fig.height=3.5}
transport |> select(mode, time_pt, time_car, time_ratio) |> pivot_longer(-mode) |>
  ggplot(aes(mode, value, fill = mode)) + geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_y") + theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = "minutes / ratio")
```

## 2. Train/test split and evaluation

```{r split}
set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(nrow(transport), floor(0.7 * nrow(transport)))
train <- transport[idx, ]; test <- transport[-idx, ]

evaluate <- function(prob_car, truth, threshold = 0.5) {
  pred <- factor(ifelse(prob_car >= threshold, "car", "public"), levels = c("public", "car"))
  sens_pt  <- mean(pred[truth == "public"] == "public")   # public-transport users found
  sens_car <- mean(pred[truth == "car"] == "car")
  c(accuracy = mean(pred == truth), `recall public` = sens_pt, `recall car` = sens_car,
    `balanced accuracy` = (sens_pt + sens_car) / 2, AUC = as.numeric(auc(truth, prob_car, quiet = TRUE)))
}
```

## 3. Random forest

A baseline forest uses 500 trees and the default `mtry` = ⌊√13⌋ = 3. Tuning then compares the out-of-bag (OOB) error over every `mtry` from 1 to 13. OOB error is computed on the trees that did not see an observation, so it serves as a built-in validation estimate without touching the test set.

```{r rf_tune, fig.height=3.5}
set.seed(123)
oob <- sapply(1:13, function(m) randomForest(mode ~ ., data = train, ntree = 500, mtry = m)$err.rate[500, "OOB"])
tibble(mtry = 1:13, `OOB error` = oob) |>
  ggplot(aes(mtry, `OOB error`)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:13) + labs(title = "Out-of-bag error by mtry")
best_mtry <- which.min(oob)
cat("best mtry:", best_mtry, "| OOB error:", round(min(oob), 4), "\n")
```

```{r rf_final}
set.seed(123)
rf <- randomForest(mode ~ ., data = train, ntree = 500, mtry = best_mtry, importance = TRUE)
rf
prob_rf <- predict(rf, test, type = "prob")[, "car"]
table(predicted = predict(rf, test), actual = test$mode)
```

```{r rf_importance, fig.height=4.5}
imp <- importance(rf, type = 1)   # mean decrease in accuracy (permutation importance)
tibble(variable = rownames(imp), importance = imp[, 1]) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(variable, importance), importance)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = "mean decrease in accuracy", title = "Random forest: permutation importance")
```

**How does the travel-time ratio shift the choice?** A partial dependence plot shows the model's average predicted log-odds of choosing the car as the ratio of public-transport to car travel time varies, with every other variable kept at its observed values:

```{r pdp, fig.height=3.5}
quantile(train$time_ratio, c(0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99))
grid <- seq(quantile(train$time_ratio, 0.01), quantile(train$time_ratio, 0.95), length.out = 40)
pdp <- sapply(grid, function(g) mean(predict(rf, mutate(train, time_ratio = g), type = "prob")[, "car"]))
ggplot(tibble(ratio = grid, p = pdp), aes(ratio, p)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_rug(data = train, aes(x = time_ratio), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(grid)) + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "public-transport time / car time", y = "average predicted P(car)",
       title = "Partial dependence on the time ratio (1st–95th percentile)")
tibble(ratio = c(1.5, 2, 3, 5)) |>
  mutate(`P(car)` = sapply(ratio, function(g) mean(predict(rf, mutate(train, time_ratio = g), type = "prob")[, "car"]))) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

## 4. Logistic regression benchmark

Logistic regression is the standard model for binary mode choice. Its coefficients are odds ratios that can be read directly. Unlike variable importance, they also give the *direction* of each effect.

```{r logit}
logit <- glm(mode ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
tidy(logit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  rename(`odds ratio` = estimate) |> kable(caption = "Logistic regression: odds of choosing the car")
prob_logit <- predict(logit, test, type = "response")
```

**Reading the odds ratios** (holding the other variables fixed):
- **Travel-time ratio:** each one-unit increase in the ratio of public-transport to car time multiplies the odds of driving by about 2.5.
- **Transfers:** one transfer raises the odds of driving by about 1.9×, multiple transfers by about 3×.
- **Walk to the stop:** a walk of more than 500 m raises them by about 1.4×.
- **Service frequency:** more than 8 departures per hour roughly *halves* the odds of driving (OR ≈ 0.52).
- **Trip length:** trips over 20 km also halve the odds (OR ≈ 0.52). These are presumably commuter-rail corridors.
- **Gender:** women have about half the odds of driving that men have (OR ≈ 0.53).
- **Other variables:** income, education, age and the transfer wait are not significant.

## 5. Comparison on the test set

```{r compare}
base_rate <- mean(train$mode == "car")
results <- rbind(
  `Always "car"`                     = evaluate(rep(base_rate, nrow(test)), test$mode, threshold = 0),
  `Logistic regression (0.5)`        = evaluate(prob_logit, test$mode),
  `Random forest (0.5)`              = evaluate(prob_rf, test$mode),
  `Random forest (threshold = share of car users)` = evaluate(prob_rf, test$mode, threshold = base_rate)
)
kable(results, digits = 3)
```

```{r roc, fig.height=4}
roc_rf <- roc(test$mode, prob_rf, quiet = TRUE); roc_lg <- roc(test$mode, prob_logit, quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_rf, col = "steelblue", main = "ROC curves (test set)"); plot(roc_lg, col = "darkorange", add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", c(sprintf("random forest (AUC %.3f)", auc(roc_rf)), sprintf("logistic (AUC %.3f)", auc(roc_lg))),
       col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"), lwd = 2)
roc.test(roc_rf, roc_lg)   # DeLong test for the AUC difference
```

## Conclusions

- **Travel-time competitiveness drives the choice.** The ratio of public-transport to car travel time is the most important predictor in the forest and the strongest effect in the logit (OR ≈ 2.5 per unit). Public transport is slower than the car for every commuter in the data (the lowest ratios are about 1.2). The partial dependence plot shows the probability of driving rising as that gap widens:
- 0.61 when public transport takes 1.5× as long as the car;
- 0.78 at 2×;
- 0.91 at 3×;
- almost no further change beyond that.

The competitive window is narrow. Public transport wins riders only when it is within about twice the car's travel time.
- **Service design matters too, in the expected direction.** Transfers and long walks to the stop push commuters into the car. High-frequency service pulls them out.
- **Prediction.**
  - Both models beat the always-"car" baseline on AUC: 0.78 for the forest and 0.77 for the logit, against 0.50.
  - At the default 0.5 threshold, though, the forest finds only 27% of public-transport users and the logit only 7%. High accuracy here mostly reflects the 85% car share.
  - Setting the threshold to the share of car users lifts recall of public-transport users to 67% and balanced accuracy from 0.62 to 0.70, at the cost of more misclassified drivers.
- **Random forest vs logit.** The forest's AUC advantage is small and not significant (DeLong p ≈ 0.66). For this problem the interpretable logit predicts about as well, and it also explains each effect.
- **Policy reading.** The largest lever is making public transport time-competitive with the car through faster, more direct and more frequent connections, with fewer transfers.
